limits: The museum says hand-formed, a regular circular foot, exterior luster and interior wear from extended tea use. The photograph does not independently distinguish use wear from firing/glaze variation; do not call it obviously broken, wholly matte, strongly asymmetric or made by Chōjirō himself. Raku ware is not automatically Wabi-sabi in every use. The connection is a documented tea-practice comparator, not a universal style certification.
observable_features: A slightly varying rim tops a largely round body that narrows and expands before reaching the small foot.
A dark undecorated surface shows tonal layers and local sheen rather than a perfectly uniform color field.
Restrained vessel form leaves these small profile and surface differences visible without a separate figurative decoration.

association_evidence.supports: The Met identifies Black Raku Tea Bowl, Kaedegure, in the style of Raku Chōjirō, 17th century, Edo period, accession 2024.553.19. It describes hand-forming, a regular carved foot, little warping, some exterior luster and interior wear from extended tea use. The attribution is not personal authorship by Chōjirō; recorded interior wear is not independently established by the selected exterior view.

Raku Museum relates the emergence of Raku tea bowls to the wabi ideals advocated by Sen Rikyū and documents Chōjirō’s foundational role in the sixteenth-century tradition. This is practice history, not authentication or a specific aesthetic judgment of the Met’s later Kaedegure bowl.

A Japanese place, neutral palette or geometrically raked garden alone would not establish those individual and time-related relationships.
